extracted.intended_audience: humor researchers, linguists, and cognitive scientists studying verbal jokes
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical framework for representing and comparing verbal jokes by decomposing them into constituent knowledge resources (parameters) and organizing those resources hierarchically to index joke variance and invariance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter 1: Language
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference in the choice of words, syntactic constructions, and other language options (phonetic, phonologic, morphophonemic, morphologic, lexic, syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic levels) that express the joke's content; a joke paraphrase is the same joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes exact wording and placement of the punchline (most jokes place the punchline in the final or prefinal position). The parameter takes input from all other parameters and is responsible for expression of casual meaning plus a joke-specific meaning. Empirical criterion for paraphrase-equivalence: a hearer will recognize a paraphrase as familiar (e.g., stop the teller). Punchlines can fail at any language level, including phonetics. (Examples: differences between jokes (1)-(3); huge paraphrase possibilities cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter 2: Narrative Strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The genre or microgenre of the joke (e.g., expository, riddle, question-and-answer, triple sequence, personal-ad format) — i.e., how the joke text is set up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different narrative strategies classify variants (e.g., (1) as a riddle/pseudoriddle vs (3) as expository). A key aspect is frequent use of nonredundancy/implicitness that creates missing links the hearer must reconstruct (deliberate violations of Grice's maxims). Examples: Q&A adaptation (9), triple sequence (11), personal-ad transformation (13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter 3: Target
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual or group at whom the joke is directed (the target); must be someone for whom the stereotyped behavior is believed to be natural (e.g., the 'dumb' stereotype).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This parameter is optional (the only optional one of the six). Suitable targets must have an associated stereotype (e.g., dumbness) which can be fictional and need not correspond to reality; the presence or absence of a target affects similarity among jokes (examples: Poles, Finns, Newfoundlanders, elephant jokes). Discussion notes ethical/empirical controversies about the relation between stereotype and real-life attitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter 4: Situation
rubrics_metrics.description: The activity, props, participants, objects, and instruments constituting what the joke is about; typically simple and obvious activities with widely known ways of doing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of situation is limited: obscure/unknown activities can incapacitate the joke for most consumers (example 18). Situations preserve similarity when they instantiate the same underlying anomalous principle even with different specific actions (examples 14–17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter 5: Logical Mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasoning pattern or mechanism that justifies the joke's incongruity (e.g., figure-ground reversal, chiasmus, analogy, garden-path/false-priming, juxtaposition/pun).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical mechanisms may be fully logical, paralogical (faulty logic), or include paralogisms and unreal elements; a joke typically provides a local or pseudological justification of the absurdity ('local logic'). Examples: figure-ground reversal in light-bulb jokes (1), chiasmus (21), garden-path/garden-path priming (24, 27), analogy (24–26), simple juxtaposition/pun (28–30). The mechanism may tolerate faulty logic because of the joke-telling communicative mode and willing suspension of disbelief; but the mechanism must provide at least a local justification to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter 6: Script Opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The script-based semantic claim that the text is compatible with two distinct scripts that are opposed; the punchline triggers a switch from one script-interpretation to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Script oppositions occur at multiple abstraction levels: most abstract (real vs unreal); lower-level manifestations include actual vs nonactual, normal vs abnormal, possible vs impossible; lowest-level oppositions include good vs bad, life vs death, sex vs nonsex, high vs low stature, etc. Different oppositions (e.g., nondumb/dumb vs clean/dirty) yield lower similarity between jokes. SSTH treated script opposition as central (and close to logical mechanisms via triggers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Knowledge Resources (KR) list
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of six knowledge resources informing a joke: script oppositions, logical mechanisms, situation, targets, narrative strategies, and language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each KR corresponds to a level in a hierarchical model of joke representation; each type of variance is indexed by one or more KRs. KRs are discovered as parameters of joke difference and can be used to define joke variants and invariants (e.g., two jokes may be variants by sharing the same script oppositions and logical mechanisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy ordering criteria for KRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles used to order the six knowledge resources into a hierarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordering is established on the basis of: (1) logical binary relations of dependence among the knowledge resources; (2) the content- vs tool-related nature of knowledge resources (content/tool dichotomy); and (3) the hypothesized perceptions of the degrees of similarity among joke examples. The model is explicitly not a model of joke production — production considerations do not inform the ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrase-equivalence empirical criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A paraphrase of a joke (different language choices expressing the same content) is considered the same joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paraphrase-equivalence is supported empirically when a hearer recognizes a paraphrase as familiar (e.g., interrupts the teller or refrains from laughing because the joke has been heard). Paraphrase space is large (many levels of language allow multiple paraphrases), and paraphrase-equivalence is grounded in semantic equivalence extended to multi-sentence jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline triggers and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Punchlines trigger script-switches and are often classified by trigger type and pulse structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two kinds of semantic script-switch triggers within the punchline: those based on an ambiguity and those based on a contradiction. Punchlines can be 'single-pulse' (straightforward) or 'rhythmic' (parallel-structured). Proper placement (final/prefinal) and wording of the punchline is crucial; other parameters operate to produce the punchline, but language realizes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonredundancy / use of implicitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of nonredundancy and implicit material in joke texts that produces missing links the hearer reconstructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phenomenon often borders on deliberate violation of Grice's maxim of quantity; it may be treated as part of narrative strategy though it also interacts with logical mechanism (inference activity). Nonredundancy contributes to the unfolding of the punchline by relying on hearer reconstruction.
